children.text: An urban park of about 58 hectares built on the site where Jose Rizal was executed, with the Rizal Monument, an honor guard, gardens, and a fountain show. Admission is free, and it connects on foot to the National Museum and Intramuros, making it the hub of a walking tour of downtown Manila.
Rizal Park is more commonly known locally by its old name, "Luneta." In Spanish times it was "Bagumbayan," an open field outside the walled city of Intramuros, and on
December 30, 1896
, Jose Rizal, the spiritual leader of the Philippine independence movement, was shot here. His death sparked the Philippine Revolution, and the park is now a symbol of Filipino national identity.
The Rizal Monument at the center of the park was completed in
, the work of Swiss sculptor Richard Kissling, chosen through an international competition. Rizal's remains are interred beneath the monument, and a Marine honor guard keeps watch over it in shifts
24 hours
a day. In front of the monument stands the "Kilometer Zero" marker, the reference point for measuring road distances across the Philippines — distances from Manila to every province start here.

The park covers about 58 hectares, with a wide lawn plaza, a Chinese Garden, a Japanese Garden, an orchidarium, and the Rizal execution-site sculptures stretching in a long line from east to west. Its west end reaches Manila Bay and its east side adjoins the National Museum complex, so it serves as the link that ties Intramuros, the National Museum, and Manila Bay together into one walking itinerary.
The name "Luneta" comes from a crescent-shaped outwork of the city's fortifications (a lunette) that once stood here. The park's history began in
, when marshland was filled in to create the Paseo de Luneta promenade, and from
, 158 people who resisted Spain were executed here. It was declared a national park in
and renamed Rizal Park in

, and it is managed by the National Parks Development Committee (NPDC) under the Department of Tourism. The park is divided into three sections: the northeast (about 16 hectares), home to the National Museum complex; the center (about 22 hectares), where the Rizal Monument and the gardens are concentrated; and the southwest (about 10 hectares), with the Quirino Grandstand and the Burnham Green lawn.

On weekends the park comes alive with families spreading out mats, joggers, and children flying kites. It's less a flashy tourist attraction than a space shared with the everyday life and history of Manila's residents, so it's recommended for travelers who want to feel the local atmosphere even on a short walk.

blocks.title: See the Rizal Monument and honor guard

children.text: In front of the monument, made up of a bronze statue and an obelisk, you can see the honor guard standing motionless at attention. The guard changes at set times, so with luck you can watch the precise ceremony up close. On the last Sunday of every month at
4 PM
, the Marine honor guard holds its official changing-of-the-guard ceremony together with a silent drill (a rifle-handling display performed without spoken commands), and anyone can watch for free.
This small marker stone on the Roxas Boulevard side in front of the monument is the reference point for road distances in the Philippines. Worth a photo if you're interested in Philippine geography.
The actual spot where Rizal was shot is not at the monument but to its north, and the execution took place at

. Here, 43 larger-than-life bronze statues re-create eight scenes, including his trial, his last meeting with his family, and the execution, alongside a black granite wall inscribed with his final poem, "Mi último adiós" ("My Last Farewell"). Every evening at
(in Filipino) and
(in English), a
30-minute
light-and-sound show is held.
The two gardens on the north side of the park are small retreats with ponds, pavilions, and bridges. The Chinese Garden was built in
with support from Taiwan and features pavilions with red pillars and green roof tiles, a statue of Confucius, and a "Path of Wisdom" inscribed with proverbs, while the Japanese Garden, opened on
, has stone lanterns, a pond, and a Japanese-style bridge. Admission is either free or a small fee, and it varies from time to time.

In the evening, a fountain show set to music and lights takes place at the pond in the center of the park. Families flock here after sunset; check the park authority's announcements for operating days and times.

blocks.title: Lapu-Lapu statue — a gift from Korea

children.text: The bronze statue "Sentinel of Freedom," about
tall, honors Lapu-Lapu, who defeated Magellan's expedition at the Battle of Mactan in
. It was donated by the Korea Freedom Federation in gratitude to the Filipino soldiers who fought in the Korean War and erected in
; after restoration, it was put back up in
August 2024
on the Maria Orosa Street side, facing the Rizal Monument.
This is the stage where the Philippines declared independence from the United States on
July 4, 1946
. The grandstand, once used for presidential inaugurations and state events, faces Manila Bay and also makes a good sunset walking route.
A white obelisk in the central section of the park marks the spot where three priests — Gomez, Burgos, and Zamora (Gomburza) — were executed by garrote on
February 17, 1872

, accused of involvement in the Cavite Mutiny. Rizal dedicated his second novel, El Filibusterismo, to these three priests, and inside the Japanese Garden there is also a marker for the "13 Martyrs of Bagumbayan," who were executed here in

The park is about
9km
from Ninoy Aquino International Airport,
30 minutes to 1 hour 20 minutes
by Grab, with a fare of about

After the
fare increase, the airport's yellow taxis (Airport Taxi) now have a flag-down rate of

Get off at United Nations Avenue station on LRT Line 1 and walk west for about
10 minutes
to reach the southeast side of the park. Getting off at Central Terminal station puts you close to the entrance on the National Museum side. The fare is about
depending on your starting station.
Take a jeepney passing along Roxas Boulevard and Taft Avenue that is marked "Luneta" or "Rizal Park." The base fare is about
, and when you want to get off, say "Para po." For first-time visitors, Grab or the LRT is far more convenient.

September 28, 2026

It's a
10–15-minute
walk from the south wall of Intramuros, and
15–25 minutes
from the Ermita/Malate hotel area. The National Museum's three buildings sit at the eastern end of the park.
From Makati it's
30 minutes to 1 hour
by Grab, costing about

(one way; more during rush hour and on rainy days). By public transport, take MRT-3 from Ayala station to Taft Avenue station, use the connecting walkway to LRT-1's EDSA station, and get off at United Nations Avenue station. BGC has no rail line, so Grab is the easiest option.
Rizal Park is about
94km
from Clark International Airport. Take a Manila-bound P2P bus from the airport (bound for NAIA, TriNoma, or Robinsons Galleria), then switch to Grab or the LRT; the bus leg alone usually takes
2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours
. Driving straight here takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
without traffic, but much longer during rush hour.
December–February
is the most pleasant, with morning and evening temperatures around 25°C, so you can walk the park for a long time without much strain.
March–May
has no rain, but midday temperatures often top 35°C, and the center of the park has little shade, so visiting after
4 PM
, once the sun starts to dip, is recommended.
During the
June–October
rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, and from
July to September
typhoons pass over Manila, bringing strong winds and heavy rain. The lawns get muddy after rain, so sneakers are more comfortable than sandals.
The park gets especially crowded on days of national events. On Independence Day (
June 12
) and Rizal Day (
December 30
), ceremonies are held and access to some areas is restricted. The Rizal Day ceremony begins with a flag-raising and wreath-laying at
7 AM
, and some lanes of Roxas Boulevard in front of the park may be closed; on the night of
December 31
, a New Year's countdown show takes place in the central section of the park. During the Black Nazarene festival (Quiapo Church) in
January
, the Pahalik, in which devotees kiss the image, continues at the Quirino Grandstand from the evening of
January 7
, and on
January 9
the Traslacion procession sets off from here at around
4 AM
, drawing hundreds of thousands of people, so avoid visiting during this period or leave plenty of time in your schedule.

Accommodation near Rizal Park clusters in the Ermita and Malate districts. The Manila Hotel on Roxas Boulevard, opened in
, is a historic hotel also known for once housing General MacArthur, priced around
a night. South of the park, several mid-range hotels along Roxas Boulevard offer Manila Bay views (around
a night), and the back streets of Malate have budget hotels and guesthouses around

Inside the park, you'll easily find stalls selling buko (young coconut) juice, fried skewers such as fishballs and kikiam, taho (a sweet snack of tofu and tapioca), and sorbetes (street ice cream). For a proper meal, we recommend Malate's Filipino restaurant row or the restaurants inside Intramuros. Enjoying afternoon tea at the Manila Hotel's café or lobby lounge is also a distinctive way to soak up its early-20th-century atmosphere.
On a pier along South Drive, west of the park, is Harbor View, a seafood restaurant in business since

, where you can enjoy garlic shrimp, squid, and fish dishes while watching the sunset over Manila Bay. For Filipino home-style cooking, we recommend The Aristocrat at the corner of Roxas Boulevard and San Andres Street, about
2km
south of the park. Running since
, it is known for its chicken barbecue with peanut sauce and Java rice, and it is open
24 hours
The park stretches over
1km
east to west, so it's efficient to start at one end and walk to the other. We recommend starting from the National Museum side and finishing at Manila Bay for the sunset.
There's little shade, so visit before
9 AM
or after
4 PM
, and bring a hat and water.
Park vendors take cash only. Carrying small bills of
and
avoids change problems.
Photos of the Rizal Monument's facade look better in the afternoon light than in the morning. The area around the monument is a protected honor-guard zone, so shoot from behind the designated line.
The fountain show and execution-site light show change days and times often, so check the official Facebook page of the National Parks Development Committee (NPDC).
Restrooms are scattered around the park, but some charge a small fee and often lack tissue, so bring your own.
Weekend afternoons are busy with local families out for the day, so choose a weekday morning if you want a quiet walk.
According to National Parks Development Committee (NPDC) announcements, the dancing fountain runs Monday to Thursday from
and Friday to Sunday from
7:00 PM to midnight
, and the light-and-sound show at the execution site has a Filipino-language showing at
and an English one at
. Some days are closed for events or maintenance, so check the
official NPDC website
When you photograph the front of the monument, the high-rise condominium Torre de Manila shows up behind it. It was dubbed the "national photobomber" for spoiling the view, but in
April 2017
the Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking its demolition, so it still stands; if you want to keep it out of your shot, photograph the monument at an angle from the side.

According to official information, the open-air auditorium on the north side of the park hosts free performances on Friday and Saturday evenings, as well as the long-running Sunday "Concert at the Park." Schedules change often, so check NPDC's official Facebook page.
Rizal Park is the largest rally venue in the Philippines. On
January 13, 2025
, a religious group's peace rally drew about 1.5 million people, and from
September 2025 to February 2026

, several anti-corruption rallies called "Baha sa Luneta" were held. On such days the park and the Roxas Boulevard area are closed off, so check the news before visiting and stay away from rally sites.
Some people approach tourists offering to take photos or act as a "guide" and then ask for money afterward. Politely decline if you don't need it.
During the crowded evening fountain shows and events, watch for pickpockets, and keep your phone and wallet in a front pocket or a bag worn in front.
Late at night (after
9 PM
), the park's outskirts and the area around the Roxas Boulevard underpass grow quiet and empty, so call a Grab and move on right away.
On days with state events, large rallies, or religious events, access may be restricted or traffic may come to a standstill, so check the news.
Entering the honor guard's monument area without authorization, or climbing on the monument, is strictly prohibited.
From
March to May
, the shadeless plazas and lawns get extremely hot at midday. The average high in April is about
and the heat index is much higher, so drink water often, and if you feel dizzy or get a headache, go indoors to rest, for example at the National Museum.
A
5-minute
walk from the park's eastern end. All three museums — art, anthropology, and natural history — are free.
A
10–15-minute
walk from the park's north side. The Spanish walled city with Fort Santiago and San Agustin Church.
A
5–10-minute
walk from the park's western end. Watch the sunset at the Roxas Boulevard Baywalk and Dolomite Beach.
About
15 minutes
by Grab. Enjoy a food trip in the world's oldest Chinatown, across the Pasig River.
About
2km
from the north side of the park, a
25–30-minute
walk. It has the Rizal Shrine, where Rizal was held until his execution, and footprint markers tracing his final steps to the execution ground, so it pairs well with a visit to Rizal Park.
